name: PowerDMARC
tagline: Hosted DMARC, SPF, DKIM and BIMI monitoring that turns raw XML aggregate reports into dashboards and alerts.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: DMARC aggregate reports are just gzipped XML emailed to an address you control, and parsing them into a per-source pass/fail table is a genuinely small program. An agent can build the ingest, the database, and a readable dashboard for your own domains in a weekend, and for one or two domains that is most of the practical value. What does not come along: forensic failure reports with their PII handling, IP and sender reputation enrichment so you can tell Mailchimp from a spoofer, SPF flattening to dodge the ten lookup limit, hosted record delegation, and BIMI certificate work that requires an actual certificate authority. You also inherit the operational judgment problem: the hard part of DMARC is deciding when it is safe to move to p=reject, not drawing the chart. Fine if you are a domain owner who wants visibility; not fine if you are an MSP billing clients for attestations.
coreLoopDIY: Pulls DMARC aggregate reports from an IMAP mailbox, unzips and parses the XML, stores per-source results in SQLite, and serves a dashboard showing which sending IPs pass SPF and DKIM alignment over time.
requirements: a domain you control and can edit DNS for
a dedicated mailbox with IMAP access for the rua address
somewhere to run a scheduled job (cron on a VPS or a laptop that is usually on)
whatYouLose: Forensic and failure reports, plus the redaction and retention policy that makes handling them legally boring
Sender reputation and IP ownership enrichment, so you get raw IPs instead of 'this is SendGrid, your marketing team'
SPF flattening and hosted record delegation, which is the thing that actually fixes the ten DNS lookup limit
BIMI and VMC issuance, which needs a certificate authority and a trademark, not code
Alerting, multi-domain tenancy, client reporting, and someone to blame when p=reject eats the invoices
moatNotes: The parsing is commodity; the surrounding services are DNS delegation, CA relationships, and being the vendor whose report an auditor accepts.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because nobody buys DMARC tooling to look at XML, they buy it to get to enforcement without blocking a payroll provider, and then to prove to an insurer or an enterprise customer that they did. A self-hosted parser answers 'what is sending as me' very well, which is genuinely most of the journey. It does not hand you a flattened SPF record, a VMC, a client-ready PDF, or a support engineer at 2am when a sanctioned mail stream starts failing alignment. Agencies managing fifty client domains are paying for the tenancy and the delegation, not the chart.
notes: The XML parser is a weekend; the nerve to publish p=reject is not.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted DMARC aggregate report dashboard. Single Python service, no cloud accounts.

Stack, non-negotiable: Python 3.11+, FastAPI, SQLite via sqlite3 (no ORM), Jinja2 templates, plain CSS, uv or pip with a requirements.txt. Server-rendered HTML only, no frontend framework, no JS build step. One small vanilla JS file is allowed for sorting tables.

What it does:
1. An ingest command (python -m dmarcbox.ingest) connects to an IMAP mailbox over SSL using credentials from .env (IMAP_HOST, IMAP_USER, IMAP_PASS, IMAP_FOLDER). It fetches unread messages, finds attachments that are .zip, .gz or .xml, decompresses them in memory, and parses the DMARC aggregate XML schema: report_metadata (org_name, report_id, date_range), policy_published (domain, p, sp, pct, adkim, aspf), and every record (source_ip, count, disposition, dkim and spf eval results, header_from, auth_results).
2. Store into SQLite tables: reports and records, with a UNIQUE constraint on (org_name, report_id) so re-ingesting is idempotent. Mark the message seen only after a successful commit. Write malformed attachments to ./quarantine/ and keep going, never crash the whole run.
3. Reverse DNS lookup each source_ip once, cache the PTR in an ip_cache table. Do not call any paid or external reputation API.
4. Web UI at /: pick a domain and a date window. Show total messages, percent fully aligned (DKIM pass OR SPF pass with alignment), and a table of sending sources sorted by volume with columns: source_ip, PTR hostname, volume, DKIM aligned %, SPF aligned %, disposition breakdown. Clicking a source shows its per-report detail rows. A second page shows the published policy over time so you can see when p changed.
5. A /sources page where you can tag an IP range as known-good with a label (e.g. 'Google Workspace'), stored in SQLite, so the dashboard can split traffic into known versus unknown. Manual tagging only.

Explicitly out of scope: forensic/RUF report parsing, SPF flattening, BIMI, DNS record editing, email alerting, multi-tenancy, auth. It binds to 127.0.0.1 and assumes you are the only user.

Deliverables: working code, requirements.txt, .env.example, a schema.sql, a sample aggregate report XML in ./fixtures/ plus a test that parses it, and a README with the exact DNS TXT record to publish (_dmarc.example.com with rua pointing at the ingest mailbox) and a crontab line to run ingest hourly. Secrets only in .env, which is gitignored. No telemetry, no analytics, no outbound calls except IMAP and DNS.
